amplification.method: the existing four-category storage accounting (Volume::storage_economics == `orfs doctor --economics`); no second accounting is invented. Authoritative = `permanent_authoritative`; manifested/derived = `rebuildable_manifestation`.

anchors.note: The identical bounded driver workload in a plain directory on the same device, with no FUSE and no WORM contract. Not a system and not ranked; it only makes the device + host-filesystem-stack cost visible.

driver.note: The driver and both daemons run as this uid. Root is used because the OrFS volume root inode is committed `0755 root:root`; the setting is identical for both arms (the sibling Go court ran as root too), so it is symmetric and changes no comparison.

differences: FUSE userspace libraries differ: OrFS-Rust serves the classical `/dev/fuse` transport through the `fuser` crate; SeaweedFS's `weed mount` uses hanwen/go-fuse/v2. Same wire protocol, independent daemons.

Backing I/O differs: OrFS-Rust writes its authoritative log locally (`--backing-io sync`); SeaweedFS's client PUTs data over loopback HTTP to a co-located volume server that writes its own `.dat` files.

Durability is NOT equal for SeaweedFS: OrFS-Rust takes one fsync per 4 KiB record (`--durability sync`, group commit OFF), while `weed mount`'s Fsync flushes the client's dirty pages to the co-located server and commits filer metadata; it is not a documented stable-storage barrier.
OrFS-Rust is mounted `--direct-io` (FOPEN_DIRECT_IO); `weed mount` exposes no such knob. Recorded, not removed.

The system arms run strictly sequentially and each system's daemon(s) and volume are released before the next system starts, so no two systems compete for the shared memory cap. All systems run in the same container caps.

Within each system the read arms run before the append arms, on a quiet volume: OrFS's append arms retain their whole history (non-withdrawal), so measuring appends first would evict the read file from the backing page cache and make every `--direct-io` read a backing I/O. All systems are measured in the same order.
`weed mount` is not SeaweedFS's fast path: its 4 KiB append+fsync rate is a legitimate result of per-record fsync through its FUSE client, not a bug.

Read caching shape differs. OrFS is mounted `--direct-io`, so every read goes through the daemon (served from the backing file's page cache); the plain-ext4 anchor serves reads from the client's own page cache; and `weed mount` serves its warm reads from an in-process chunk cache. The SeaweedFS 4 KiB read rows therefore include client cache hits (a ~271 ns p50 is not a backing read), which is why its read shape is not the same data path as the others'.

OrFS-Rust's per-record durable commit is serialized when group commit is off (this court's contract): at 64 writers the append arm does not scale (one fsync barrier per transaction, taken under the commit lock), while the same device in a plain directory sustains 64 concurrent native writers far higher. This is a measured property of the equal-durability OrFS setting, not a device limit.

The two OrFS-Rust append rows share ONE durability contract — an acknowledged record is durable (its covering barrier completed). They differ only in whether the opt-in group-commit coordinator amortises that barrier over a batch: `group commit on` (--group-commit, adaptive linger) lets concurrently-arrived mutations and fsync(2) share one barrier per batch, so it is the same contract delivered at a lower barrier frequency, not a weaker one.
Host-level variance (page cache state, scheduler, backing-device write cache) is not controlled beyond the shared container; run-to-run variance is expected and unquantified here.

not_comparable.reason: The driver issues write(2)+fsync(2) per 4 KiB record on both, but only OrFS-Rust implements fsync as a durable barrier (one fsync of the authoritative log per record). SeaweedFS 3.99's FUSE client implements Fsync as a flush of dirty pages to the co-located volume server plus a filer metadata commit, with no fsync of the volume `.dat` or the filer store. The SeaweedFS append rows are therefore NOT equal-durability with the OrFS rows and must not be read as such.

SeaweedFS is a client/server filesystem: even co-located, the FUSE client's data crosses the loopback network stack (HTTP) to the volume server and its metadata crosses gRPC to the filer, unlike the local in-process OrFS daemon.

OrFS retains every committed transition as an enumerable, readable historical root (non-withdrawal); `weed mount` exposes no snapshot or historical-root interface. The retention axis is not comparable and is recorded, never faked.

The identical pread workload crosses three different read paths: OrFS (direct-io, daemon-served from the backing page cache), the plain ext4 anchor (client page cache), and `weed mount` (an in-process client chunk cache that answers warm reads without a backing round trip). The rows are published as measured; a cache hit and a backing read are not the same operation.
The ZFS and Btrfs arms did not run in this container (see the `probes` block for each concrete reason). No ZFS or Btrfs measurement is implied.

`anchors` holds the same bounded workload in a plain directory on the same device, with no FUSE and no WORM contract. It exists only to make the device's own cost visible; it is not a WORM system and is not ranked against the `rows`.

comparability.note: Two mounted storage systems driven by one shared driver on the same machine and device. Durability is equal-by-construction for OrFS-Rust (one fsync per record) but NOT for SeaweedFS (flush-to-server, not a stable-storage barrier) — its append rows are published but must not be read as equal-durability. No row is a ranking.

group_commit_off.role: the equal-durability baseline; every sync transaction pays its own fsync

group_commit_on.note: same driver, same device, same durability contract (an acknowledged record is durable); only the barrier is amortised
group_commit_on.role: OrFS's best honest configuration for per-record durable appends; concurrently-arrived mutations and fsync(2) share one barrier per batch, but every acknowledged record is still covered by a completed barrier

workload.append_durability: write(2)+fsync(2) per record (one durability barrier per record)

container_tmp.note: A device baseline only. A per-record durable append cannot be faster than its durable barrier, so compare an append arm's mean latency against this, not against another system's.
container_tmp.operation: write(2) of 4096 bytes + fsync(2), 64 samples, outside any mount

evidence_volume_device.note: A device baseline only. A per-record durable append cannot be faster than its durable barrier, so compare an append arm's mean latency against this, not against another system's.
evidence_volume_device.operation: write(2) of 4096 bytes + fsync(2), 64 samples, outside any mount

device_baseline.load_caveat: This is a single-run figure on a shared host: a raw fsync stalls when the drive's write queue is saturated, so it moves materially between runs. It is recorded, not curated; read it as an order of magnitude, not a constant.
device_baseline.note: `evidence_volume_device` is where THIS court's OrFS and SeaweedFS volumes live. `container_tmp` is the container's own writable layer (TMPDIR) — the path the sibling Go court used — recorded so the two receipts' absolute append numbers are not confused with each other.

note: A same-machine open-source WORM comparison: a shared, bounded driver (this test) drove MOUNTED storage implementations on the same machine, the same device and the same container caps. This receipt is data, not a leaderboard: rows are keyed by {system, workload, writers, readers, block_size} and are never ranked across incomparable coordinates. Durability is a per-system property recorded in the comparability block, not a claim this note makes for every row. A local FUSE read, an internal transaction path, and a distributed object store are different interfaces. Read the comparability block, including `not_comparable`, before drawing any conclusion.
notes: Every row is one bounded arm of the shared driver against a MOUNTED filesystem on this machine.
OrFS-Rust is mounted through the real `orfs mount` code path (`fuse::spawn`) as a separate daemon process, with `--direct-io --durability sync --backing-io sync` and group commit OFF.
SeaweedFS 3.99 is staged from the pinned image (digest recorded) and run as `weed server` + `weed mount` on loopback with GOGC/GOMEMLIMIT bounded; `weed mount` is not its fast path.

The retention axis enumerates every committed transaction boundary of a dedicated OrFS volume and opens/reads a bounded sample of them as historical views; total physical amplification comes from the existing four-category accounting.

The evidence volumes live on the bind-mounted host drive (the recorded backing filesystem); `device_baseline` records that device's own 4 KiB write+fsync cost, because a per-record durable append cannot be faster than its barrier.
The ZFS and Btrfs arms are recorded as `measured: false` with a concrete probed reason, never implied.
The receipt carries no ranking: two rows are comparable only at the same {workload, writers, readers, block_size} under the listed configuration differences.
